title: Ipswich chairman apologises ‘unreservedly’ for ‘hurt and pain’ caused by Nigel Farage visit
content:
The chairman and chief executive of Ipswich Town has apologised “unreservedly” for the “hurt, pain and frustration” caused by a visit to the club’s stadium from right-wing politician Nigel Farage.

In a video published on the club’s website, Mark Ashton said Ipswich had “lessons to learn” from the episode, and revealed their board of directors were currently in the process of reviewing their policy towards politicians and political parties.

Farage, the leader of Reform UK and long-time ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, visited Ipswich’s Portman Road stadium on Monday. Farage posed for photos and posted a video of himself wishing the club luck in their bid to be promoted to the Premier League this season.

“I am fully aware that this has been a very difficult week for all of us,” Ashton said. “The staff are hurting, elements of the fanbase are hurting, and so are elements of our local community. And that upsets me immensely. And for that, unreservedly, I want to apologise and say I’m sorry.

“I understand that supporters and elements of the community are angry. I also understand that there are a number of mistruths out there on what’s actually happened this week, and I also understand that we have lessons to learn. Mistakes have been made which have caused harm and distress to part of our local community. As chairman of the club, I take full responsibility for those mistakes and full responsibility for making sure those lessons are learned and learnt quickly.”

On Tuesday morning, by which point Farage’s visit had led to a significant backlash, Ipswich told The Athletic that the politician had not been formally invited to their ground.

The Athletic, however, has reported that the invitation to Farage and his political party was extended by an associate of Ashton, who had lunch with the divisive politician, along with the club’s chief operating officer Luke Werhun.

The Athletic also reported that Ipswich gifted the politician six of their replica shirts with ‘Farage, 10’ printed on the backs free of charge (10 Downing Street in central London is where the sitting UK prime minister lives), and that members of staff, some senior, have made formal complaints to their human resources department over the matter.

In his message, Ashton said that the board was reviewing “how, if and when” the club would engage with politicians or political parties in future, and acknowledged that the episode had “dented an element of the trust and faith we have between the club and its fanbase”.

The Ipswich chairman and CEO, who did not mention Farage or the visit specifically, urged the club to move forward “as one”.

“There’s lots to fight for, on and off the pitch, as we move forward and I felt we’ve always been better as we move forward as one,” Ashton said.

“We do try to listen to supporters, and we do take on board their feelings and thoughts on wide-ranging things and the biggest thing this week has been the hurt and frustration that fans have had. And again, I repeat, I unreservedly apologise for that hurt and pain. I’m genuinely sorry.”

On Friday, Farage claimed he has been invited by Sunderland of the Premier League to visit their Stadium of Light.

“I’ve been talking to one of the directors, and they’d very much like to see me there,” he said, per ITV. “If I can make it, I will. Clubs should want to talk to me.”
